source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Greenway_2024_MusicKetamineRCT.pdf, version of record, JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(2):e2354719, 4 printed pages, all read; Figures 1 and 2 checked on a 300-dpi render of p. 2. The three supplements (protocol and analysis plan, eMethods and eTables, data-sharing statement) and the registry record were not in the folder and were not read.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim keeps the finding to blood pressure, says the letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt or on depression, and does not call the difference a clinical benefit; the causal wording ('found a smaller rise with music') is carried by the randomized design.
claims.note: Every number from this source checks out. The editors' reading of Figure 2A (about 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg) matches the render, and Figure 2B shows both arms starting at about 119.6 mm Hg and reaching about 131 (music) and 138 (no music) at 40 minutes, a raw gap of about 7.4. The claim's inference of 31 patients analysed for the primary outcome follows from the flow diagram (15 + 16). The transposed-signs reading of the diastolic interval is right: -1.59 to 3.18 is centred on +0.8, and Figure 2A shows the diastolic rise slightly smaller with music.

anchors.extracted: MUSIK randomized clinical trial, Montreal, January 2021 to August 2022, NCT04701866, ethics approval from two institutes, CONSORT-reported. Patients had a current unipolar or bipolar depressive episode refractory to at least 2 adequate medication trials and had been accepted for intravenous ketamine treatment. Randomized 1:1 to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion or to usual care without music, during a course of 6 subanaesthetic doses (0.5 mg/kg) over 4 weeks (treatment conditions). Primary outcome: change in systolic blood pressure, the difference between the mean of triplicate readings at 0 and at 40 minutes of each infusion, 40 minutes chosen in advance as the time of peak plasma values. Generalized estimating equations across all 6 infusions, intention to treat with inverse-probability weighting for missing data; the sample-size calculation estimated 30 patients.

32 patients enrolled, 15 to music and 17 to usual care; 23 (72%) women, mean age 45.9 (SD 14.2), 27 (84%) White; no serious adverse events recorded; 28 completed the trial per protocol. Flow: 40 assessed, 8 excluded (2 active substance use disorder, 4 episodes not meeting resistance criteria, 2 declined). Music arm: 1 lost to 8-week follow-up, 1 excluded from the study for violating the clinic's safety protocol, 15 analysed for the primary outcome. Usual care: 1 lost to follow-up, 3 discontinued (1 chose music, 1 psychoactive effects, 1 worsening illness), 16 in the corresponding box with 1 excluded from analysis and no reason given.

181 infusions administered (87 music, 94 no music). Population-averaged effects: music reduced the rise in systolic blood pressure, beta -7.4 mm Hg (95% CI -12.0 to -2.9), P = .008; diastolic beta -0.8 mm Hg (95% CI printed -1.59 to 3.18), P = .58. Editors' check: the systolic interval implies a standard error of about 2.3 and a Wald p near 0.001, smaller than the printed .008; the diastolic interval is not centred on its point estimate.

anchors.locator: Figure 2, panels A and B (300-dpi render)
anchors.extracted: Panel A, mean change over the infusion across 181 infusions: systolic about 11.5 mm Hg with music against about 18.5 without; diastolic about 7.6 against about 8.1; error bars are 95% CIs. Panel B, raw mean systolic pressure: about 119.6 mm Hg at 0 minutes in both arms, about 125 (music) and 132 (no music) at 15 minutes, and about 131 against 138 at 40 minutes.

The authors state, citing an expert-opinion paper, that up to 20% of patients receiving intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression require pharmacological management of treatment-induced hypertension, and that music has improved the haemodynamic response of other medical interventions but had not been studied for ketamine in this condition. The trial reports no per-arm count of patients needing such treatment.

The authors conclude that music significantly decreased ketamine-induced systolic changes and may be a feasible, benign, non-pharmacological approach; secondary trial outcomes will be published elsewhere; they suggest ketamine's psychoactive effects may amplify the effects of music and other environmental influences, and name the modest sample as a limitation. No experience, dissociation or depression outcome appears anywhere in the letter, and the comparison was with usual care, without any sound or attention control.

key_findings.note: Race counts sum to 32 (27 White, 2 Hispanic, 1 Asian, 1 Black, 1 Middle Eastern).
I reproduced the editors' Wald check: systolic SE about 2.32, z about 3.19, p about 0.001 against the printed .008; the diastolic interval implies p about 0.51 against the printed .58.
Figure readings re-taken independently on a 300-dpi render and they agree within the width of a marker.

reporting_issues.note: An interval centred on +0.795; Figure 2A shows the diastolic rise slightly lower with music, so the point estimate's sign is the plausible one.
Recomputed: systolic z about 3.19 (p about 0.0014), diastolic z about 0.66 (p about 0.51).

Confirmed on the render: the usual-care box at the primary-outcome stage is labelled 'Analyzed for secondary outcome measures', duplicating the row below, so the primary-outcome denominator for that arm is never stated; 15 + 16 = 31 is the only available reading.
Accepted for Publication: December 13, 2022; analyses conducted September 2022 to July 2023; published February 5, 2024.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 fits a parallel-group randomized trial, and 'some concerns' overall matches the worst domains. The domains rest partly on what the letter omits rather than on what it did, which the card states; the supplements, if read, could lower several of them.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' fits: the results are reported plainly, and the stretch is the word 'improving' without any clinical outcome, which the card records.

missed: The flow diagram counts patients 'lost to 8-week follow-up' in both arms, so the trial followed patients beyond the 4-week infusion course; the letter reports nothing from that follow-up, which reinforces the card's point that all non-haemodynamic outcomes are deferred.
The title and discussion speak of the haemodynamic response, but only blood pressure is reported: no heart rate or other haemodynamic measure appears in the letter.
